py.u03.title: Keep guessing
py.u03.description: Let the player keep guessing the secret number until they get it right.
py.u03.learn: A while loop repeats a block of code for as long as its condition is True. Python checks the condition, runs the indented block, then checks again. When the condition becomes False, the loop ends and the program carries on below it.
py.u03.detail: Something inside the loop must change, or the condition stays True forever. To keep asking the player, call input() once before the loop and again at the end of the block. If the condition is False the very first time, the block never runs at all.
py.u03.example:
# Keep asking until the password is moon
word = input("Password? ")
while word != "moon":
    print("The door stays shut.")
    word = input("Password? ")
print("The door opens.")
py.u03.exampleOutput:
The door stays shut.
The door stays shut.
The door opens.
py.u03.exampleNote: The condition is checked before each repeat. star and sun are not moon, so the block runs twice. When word becomes moon, the condition is False, the loop ends, and the last line runs.
py.u03.question: If the first reply were moon, what would the program print?
options: The door stays shut. once, then The door opens.
py.u03.why: word != "moon" is False straight away, so the block never runs. Python goes on to the last line and prints The door opens.
py.u03.guided: Run it, then change the replies so that moon comes first, then last. Predict how many times The door stays shut. appears before each run. Then try three wrong replies and read what happens when the replies run out.
py.u03.starter:
# These two lines ask for the secret number and the first guess
secret = int(input("Secret number? "))
guess = int(input("Your guess? "))
# While the guess is wrong: print whether it is too high, then ask again
py.u03.challenge: The riddle keeper lets the player keep guessing. The starter asks for the secret number and the first guess. While the guess is wrong, print True if it is too high or False if it is too low, then ask for another guess. When the guess is right, the loop ends. Print just the True and False lines. The check tries several runs of guesses, including some you can't see.
hints: You need a loop that repeats while the guess is not the secret. Inside it, two things happen: a print() and a new guess.
Look at the comment. The loop's condition compares guess with secret using !=. The last line inside the loop asks for the next guess, the same way the starter asked for the first one.
A pattern from the worked example: while word != "moon": with an indented print(), then an indented line that asks again. Your loop compares numbers instead of words.

errorHints.text: Your loop asked for another guess after the last reply. Check that it stops as soon as the guess is right: that is when its condition should become False.
Use the names from the starter, secret and guess, and spell them the same inside the loop.
The lines inside the loop start with four spaces, so Python knows they belong to it.
Each new guess needs int(...) too, like the first one. Python can't compare text with a number using >.
With a secret of 7 and guesses of 9, 3 and 7, the lines are True, then False. If only True printed, your program checked once with if; a while loop checks again after every guess.
When the first guess is right, the loop never runs and nothing is printed. If your program printed a line, check that the print() is inside the loop.
Three low guesses print three False lines. Make sure your loop keeps going for as long as the guess is wrong, however many guesses that takes.
Guesses below zero compare the same way. Compare guess with secret, not with particular numbers.
Your loop needs to keep going for as many wrong guesses as the player makes, not for a fixed number of them.

similarExample.code:
steps = 1
while steps < 50:
    steps = steps * 3
print(steps)
similarExample.note: The loop keeps tripling steps while it is under 50: 1, 3, 9, 27, then 81. 81 < 50 is False, so the loop stops and 81 is printed. Your challenge repeats while a guess is wrong, and asks for a new guess each time.

otherWays.code:
secret = int(input("Secret number? "))
guess = int(input("Your guess? "))
while guess != secret:
    too_high = guess > secret
    print(too_high)
    guess = int(input("Your guess? "))
otherWays.note: Keep the answer in a variable, then print it.
while True repeats until break leaves the loop, so input() is written only once. The next lesson looks at how loops end.

py.u03.title: Three tries
py.u03.description: Give the player three tries, and make sure the loop always ends.
py.u03.learnTitle: Every loop needs a way out
py.u03.learn: A loop ends only when its condition becomes False. Something inside the loop has to move it there: a counter that goes up or down, or a new reply. If nothing changes, the loop runs forever.
py.u03.detail: A counter often decides how many times a loop runs. Starting it at 0 or at 1, and choosing < or <=, changes the count by one. To stop for either of two reasons, join the conditions with and: keep going while the guess is wrong and tries are left. Here, a program that never ends is stopped for you after a few seconds.
py.u03.example:
# Count down to the gate opening
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1
print("open")
py.u03.exampleNote: count goes 3, 2, 1. After 1 is printed it becomes 0, so count > 0 is False and the loop ends. The last line runs once, after the loop.
py.u03.question: If the line count = count - 1 were deleted, what would happen?
options: It would still print 3, 2, 1 and open
It would print 3 again and again and never finish
Python would stop with an error at once
py.u03.why: count would stay 3, so count > 0 would always be True and the loop would never end. Because it prints each time, the academy stops it as soon as the output gets too long. You can try it on the next card.
py.u03.guided: Predict, then run: change count = 3 to count = 5. Next, delete the line count = count - 1 and run it; the academy stops the program and explains why. Put the line back with Reset code. Last, change > to >= and count how many numbers print.
py.u03.starter:
# Ask for the secret number and the first guess
# Keep asking while the guess is wrong and tries are left
# Then print the number of guesses, and whether the last one was right
py.u03.challenge: The riddle keeper allows three tries. Ask for the secret number, then ask for guesses until the guess is right or three guesses have been made. After the loop, print two lines: how many guesses were made, then True if the last guess was right or False if it was not. Print just the two answers.
hints: Count the guesses as you go. The loop needs two reasons to keep going, joined with and: the guess is wrong, and fewer than three guesses have been made.
Check your counter: after the first guess it should be 1. Each time the loop asks again, add 1. With three tries, the loop can ask at most two more times.
A pattern with other names: while answer != key and turns < 5: with indented lines that ask again and add 1 to turns.

errorHints.text: Your loop asked for another guess after the last reply. It should stop after three guesses, even when none of them is right: check the counter in the loop's condition.
Give every name a value before the loop uses it, including the counter, and spell it the same each time.
Here the third guess is right, so the lines are 3 and True. If your program stopped after two guesses, check where your counter starts and whether you used < or <=.
Three wrong guesses use up the tries, so the second line is False. Print whether the last guess equals the secret, rather than True every time.
When the first guess is right, the loop never runs: one guess, and True. Check that your counter is 1 after the first guess.
Only the first three guesses count, so the lines are 3 and False, even though a fourth reply would be right. If your program printed 4 and True, the loop needs a limit on tries.
Count every guess, including the first one, so the number printed is right whichever try solves the riddle.
A secret below zero works the same way. Compare the guess with the secret instead of checking for particular numbers.

similarExample.code:
fuel = 10
trips = 0
while fuel >= 3 and trips < 2:
    fuel = fuel - 3
    trips = trips + 1
print(trips)
print(fuel)
similarExample.note: The cart keeps going while there is fuel for a trip and fewer than 2 trips are done. Both reasons are checked each time, and the loop stops when either one fails: here after 2 trips, with 4 fuel left. Your challenge stops when the guess is right or the tries run out.

otherWays.code:
secret = int(input("Secret number? "))
guess = int(input("Your guess? "))
tries = 1
while guess != secret and tries < 3:
    guess = int(input("Your guess? "))
    tries += 1
print(tries)
print(guess == secret)
otherWays.note: tries += 1 is a short way to write tries = tries + 1.

otherWays.code:
secret = int(input("Secret number? "))
tries = 0
while tries < 3:
    guess = int(input("Your guess? "))
    tries = tries + 1
    if guess == secret:
        break
print(tries)
print(guess == secret)
otherWays.note: A loop that counts to three, with break to leave early when the guess is right.

py.u03.title: Step by step
py.u03.description: Count the steps of a staircase with a for loop and range(), two at a time.
py.u03.learn: A for loop runs its block once for each value it is given. range(1, 4) gives 1, 2 and 3: it starts at the first number and stops before the second. So for n in range(1, 4): with print(n) inside prints 1, 2 and 3.
py.u03.detail: range(4) on its own gives 0, 1, 2 and 3. A third number sets the step: range(2, 9, 2) gives 2, 4, 6 and 8, and a step of -1 counts down. To include a number at the end, make the stop one bigger. A for loop moves its own variable on each time, so it always ends.
py.u03.exampleNote: range(1, 6) stops before 6, so the planks are 1 to 5. A step of -1 counts down: range(3, 0, -1) gives 3, 2 and 1, and stops before 0.
py.u03.question: What would for n in range(2, 7, 2): with print(n) inside print?
py.u03.why: It starts at 2 and adds 2 each time: 2, 4, 6. The next number would be 8, but range stops before 7, so 8 is never reached.
py.u03.guided: Predict, then run: change range(1, 6) to range(1, 11). Then make the countdown start at 10. Last, change the countdown's step to -2 and predict the numbers before you run.
py.u03.starter: # Ask for the top step, then print every step the hero lands on
py.u03.challenge: The hero climbs the riddle keeper's staircase two steps at a time, starting on step 2. Ask for the number of the top step, then print every step the hero lands on, up to and including the top step if they land on it. Print just the step numbers, one per line.
hints: The hero lands on 2, 4, 6 and so on. A for loop over a range() with a step of 2 gives exactly those numbers.
range() stops before its second number. For a top step of 8, the stop has to be bigger than 8, or step 8 is missed.
A pattern with other names: for seat in range(1, rows + 1, 3): gives 1, 4, 7 and so on, up to rows. Your loop starts at a different number and steps by 2.

errorHints.text: range() needs whole numbers. Turn the reply into a number with int(...) before you use it.
Use the same name for the top step everywhere, and give it a value with input() before the loop.
The line inside the for loop starts with four spaces.
With a top step of 8, the hero lands on 2, 4, 6 and 8. If 8 is missing, the stop of your range() is 8: make it one bigger.
With a top step of 7, the hero lands on 2, 4 and 6, never on 8, which is above the top. Check the stop of your range().
With a top step of 1, the hero never lands on a step, so nothing is printed. A range() that starts above its stop gives no numbers at all.
Use the reply in your range(), not numbers typed into the code, so it works for every staircase.
Check odd top steps as well as even ones: the last step printed is the biggest even number that is not above the top.

similarExample.note: Starting at floor 10 and going down 3 at a time gives 10, 7, 4 and 1. The stop, 0, is never printed. Your challenge counts up by 2 and has to reach the top step.

otherWays.code:
top = int(input("Top step? "))
step = 2
while step <= top:
    print(step)
    step = step + 2
otherWays.note: The same steps with a while loop. for and range() do the counting for you, so they are the tidy way, but this works too.
Go through every step and print only the even ones: step % 2 == 0 means no remainder after dividing by 2.

py.u03.title: Keep the score
py.u03.description: Add up the points from every round of the riddle keeper's game, count the empty rounds, and find the average.
py.u03.learnTitle: Build up an answer, one turn at a time
py.u03.learn: A running total starts at 0 before the loop. Inside the loop, total = total + coins adds this turn's number to what is already there. When the loop ends, total holds the sum of them all.
py.u03.detail: A counter works the same way, but adds 1 each time something happens, often inside an if. The start line goes above the loop, so it runs once: inside the loop it would wipe the total every turn. For an average, divide the total by how many numbers there were, after the loop.
py.u03.example:
# Three chests: add up the coins, then find the average
chests = 3
total = 0
for chest in range(chests):
    coins = int(input("Coins in this chest? "))
    total = total + coins
print(total)
print(total / chests)
py.u03.exampleNote: total starts at 0 and grows: 4, then 4 again, then 12. The two print lines are below the loop, not indented, so they run once, after the last chest. Dividing with / always gives a float, so the average shows as 4.0.
py.u03.question: Suppose total = 0 moves inside the loop, as the first line of its block. With the same replies, what would print(total) show?
py.u03.why: total goes back to 0 at the start of every turn, so each chest forgets the ones before it. Only the last chest's 8 is left when the loop ends.
py.u03.guided: Predict, then run: move total = 0 inside the loop, as the first line of its block, and check your prediction. Put it back above the loop. Then add a counter for empty chests: start it above the loop, add 1 inside an if, and print it at the end.
py.u03.starter: # Ask for the rounds, then the points from each round
py.u03.challenge: The riddle keeper's game now has rounds. Ask how many rounds were played (always at least 1), then ask for the points from each round. Print three lines: the total points, how many rounds scored 0, and the average points per round, using /. Print just the numbers.
hints: You need two things that build up as the loop runs, and both start at 0 above the loop: one for the points, and one for the rounds that scored 0.
A for loop over range() runs once per round. Ask for that round's points inside it. The three print lines go after the loop, with no indent.
A pattern with other names: start with distance = 0, and inside the loop use distance = distance + miles. Your loop also needs a counter, and an if to decide when it goes up.

errorHints.text: A reply from input() is text. Turn it into a number with int(...) before you add it up or use it in range().
Give each name a value before the loop uses it, and spell it the same way every time.
The lines that repeat start with four spaces. A line inside an if inside the loop starts with eight.
Your loop asked for more points than there were rounds. range(rounds) already runs exactly once per round.
The average divides by the number of rounds played, and that is always at least 1. Check which number comes after the /.
With one round of 10 points, the lines are 10, 0 and 10.0. A total or a counter that starts above 0 is already wrong here, and // gives 10 where / gives 10.0.
With rounds of 10, 0 and 5, the lines are 15, 1 and 5.0. If your total says 5, it goes back to 0 on every turn: its start line belongs above the loop.
With two rounds of 0, the lines are 0, 2 and 0.0. Every round that scores 0 counts, even when nothing has been scored yet.
Check a longer game: use the number of rounds in range() and in the average, and / rather than //, which throws away the part after the point.
Check a game with more than one empty round: the counter goes up every time a round scores 0.

similarExample.code:
gold = 1
for day in range(3):
    gold = gold * 2
print(gold)
similarExample.note: Another answer that builds up: the gold doubles each day, giving 8 after three days. It starts at 1, because doubling 0 would stay 0. Your challenge adds up every round and counts the empty ones instead.

otherWays.code:
rounds = int(input("Rounds? "))
total = 0
empty = 0
count = 0
while count < rounds:
    points = int(input("Points? "))
    total = total + points
    if points == 0:
        empty = empty + 1
    count = count + 1
print(total)
print(empty)
print(total / rounds)
otherWays.note: The same totals with a while loop, which needs its own count of the rounds so far. for and range() do that counting for you.

otherWays.code:
rounds = int(input("Rounds? "))
total = 0
scored = 0
for game in range(rounds):
    points = int(input("Points? "))
    total += points
    if points > 0:
        scored += 1
print(total)
print(rounds - scored)
print(total / rounds)
otherWays.note: Count the rounds that scored instead, and take them away from all the rounds. += is a short way to write total = total + points.

py.u03.title: Rooms on the map
py.u03.concept: Loops · a loop inside a loop
py.u03.description: Walk the riddle keeper's map row by row, count the coins in each room, and add them all up.
py.u03.learnTitle: Put a loop inside a loop
py.u03.learn: A loop's block can hold another loop. The inner loop runs all the way through, every time the outer loop goes round once. So an outer loop of 2 turns and an inner loop of 3 turns runs the inner block 6 times.
py.u03.detail: The outer loop's line starts at the left, the inner loop's line has four spaces, and the inner block has eight. for and range() start the inner loop again by themselves. With while, the inner counter has to be set back to its start inside the outer loop, or the inner loop only runs the first time.
py.u03.exampleNote: row starts at 1, and seat runs through 1, 2 and 3. Then row becomes 2, and seat starts again from 1. Multiplying by 10 is just a way to show both numbers at once: 23 is row 2, seat 3.
py.u03.question: If the two for lines swapped places, so that seat is the outer loop and row the inner one, what would the first three lines print?
py.u03.why: The inner loop finishes first. seat stays at 1 while row runs through 1 and 2, giving 11 and 21. Then seat becomes 2 and row starts again, giving 12.
py.u03.guided: Predict, then run: swap the two for lines, with row and seat keeping their ranges. Put them back. Then change range(1, 3) to range(1, 4) and predict how many lines print before you run.
py.u03.starter: # Ask for the rows and the columns, then walk the map
py.u03.challenge: The riddle keeper's map is a grid of rooms. Rows and columns are counted from 1, and a room holds its row number times its column number in coins, so row 2, column 3 holds 6. Ask for the number of rows, then the number of columns. Going through the rows in order, and left to right along each row, print the coins in every room, one per line. On the last line, print the total coins. Print just the numbers.
hints: One for loop goes through the rows. Inside its block, another for loop goes through the columns of that row.
Rows and columns count from 1, and range() stops before its second number. The total starts at 0 above both loops, and prints below both of them.
A pattern with other names: for shelf in range(1, shelves + 1): holds for book in range(1, books + 1): one step further in. The rooms need your own names, your own sum, and a total.

errorHints.text: range() needs whole numbers. Turn each reply into a number with int(...) before you use it.
Use one name for the rows and one for the columns, and give each a value with input() before the loops.
Each loop's block goes four spaces further in than its for line: four for the inner for line, and eight for the lines inside it.
This program needs only two replies, the rows and the columns. Ask for them once, above the loops.

With 2 rows of 3 columns, the coins go 1, 2, 3, then 2, 4, 6, and the total is 18. If you see 1, 2, 2, 4, 3, 6, the two loops are the wrong way round. If only the first row printed, the inner counter did not start again.
With 3 rows of 2 columns, the coins go 1, 2, then 2, 4, then 3, 6. Use the replies in your range() calls, not numbers typed into the code.
A map of one room holds 1 coin, so the lines are 1 and then the total, 1. The total line is always printed.
Check a map with more rows than the examples: the outer range() has to follow the rows reply.
Check a map with more columns than the examples: the inner range() has to follow the columns reply.

similarExample.note: A clock that strikes every half hour shows 100, 130, 200 and 230: for each hour, the minutes start again from 0. Your challenge goes through rows and columns, counts from 1, and adds everything up.

otherWays.code:
rows = int(input("Rows? "))
columns = int(input("Columns? "))
total = 0
row = 1
while row <= rows:
    column = 1
    while column <= columns:
        print(row * column)
        total = total + row * column
        column = column + 1
    row = row + 1
print(total)
otherWays.note: The same walk with while loops. Look at column = 1: it sits inside the outer loop, so each row starts again from the first column. for and range() do that for you.

otherWays.code:
rows = int(input("Rows? "))
columns = int(input("Columns? "))
total = 0
for room in range(rows * columns):
    row = room // columns + 1
    column = room % columns + 1
    print(row * column)
    total = total + row * column
print(total)
otherWays.note: One loop over every room, working out its row and column with // and %. It is correct and clever, but two loops say what you mean more plainly.
